### Shoulder Girdle and Upper Limb.

The SH glenoid cavity is consistently taller and narrower (_n_ = 10) than in MH, reflected in a low glenoid index ([_SI Appendix_, Fig. S6 and Tables S13–S16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). The SH sample shows a dominant dorsal position (_n_ = 8) of the axillary sulcus for the _Musculus teres minor_ (on the axillary border), resembling the predominant condition in Neandertals. Only one specimen (Scapula IV) displays a ventral sulcus (the most frequent condition in MH).

The curvatures of the SH clavicles in the transverse plane fall within the normal variation in MH. Nevertheless, the curvatures in the coronal plane, in all of the SH specimens where it can be determined, are of type II, as is the case in all Neandertals that we have studied and the few known early Pleistocene specimens. In contrast, MH show three curvature types ([31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r31)).

Most of the SH humeri display a consistent morphological pattern that distinguishes them from MH and is similar to Neandertals. This pattern includes a transversely oval humeral head, a projected and massive lesser trochanter, a narrower deltoid tuberosity with two muscular crests, thick cortical diaphyses ([Fig. 1 _E_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01)), a broader and deeper olecranon fossa, a relatively narrower medial distal pillar surrounding the olecranon fossa ([Fig. 2 _B_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig02)), a rectangular and broader capitulum, and a shallower trochlea with a less projecting lateral rim. In these two latter traits, the specimens show some variation.

The ulnae have a broader olecranon process, an anterior orientation of the trochlear notch (the plesiomorphic condition for all hominins), a vertically extended radial notch, a short and blunt supinator crest, a robust pronator crest, a blunt interosseous crest, a rounded and gracile diaphysis and pronounced antero-posterior (AP) and ML shaft curvature ([_SI Appendix_, Fig. S7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). This pattern is also present in the Neandertals and distinguishes them from MH ([_SI Appendix_, Tables S13–S16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).

Most of the SH radii (six of eight specimens) display a relatively long and gracile neck, an antero-medially oriented radial tuberosity, and a low robusticity index with a pronounced ML shaft curvature, as in the Neandertals. However, two SH specimens show the relatively short and robust neck, anteriorly oriented radial tuberosity, and the straight and robust shaft typical of MH ([_SI Appendix_, Fig. S8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).

### Hand.

The SH hand is characterized by a strong development of the palmar tubercles of the carpal bones associated with a deep carpal tunnel (palmar projections of the tubercle of the trapezium and the hamulus) ([Fig. 1 _F_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01)); high mobility of the first metacarpal (MC1), reflected in the saddle-shaped carpo-metacarpal articulation of the thumb; high capacity for rotation of the second metacarpal (MC2); robust thumbs with a strong attachment for the _Musculus opponens pollicis_ ([Fig. 2 _C_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig02)), relatively short proximal phalanges, and relatively long distal phalanges; noncurved proximal and middle phalanges with relatively broad trochleae; distal phalanges with expanded distal tuberosities; pea-shaped pisiforms; and relatively short (proximo-distal) lunates and relatively broad (radio-ulnar) triquetrals ([_SI Appendix_, Table S17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). The SH hand morphology indicates a powerful precision grip and fine precision grasping capabilities that are similar to what has been described in Neandertals ([39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r39)) and MH. In the SH hand, like in Neandertals, the powerful precision grip is enhanced by the thumb robusticity and well-developed flexor musculature.

### Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limb.

The SH pelvises are characterized by their marked robusticity (e.g., large sacroiliac joint, iliac tubercle, and ischial tuberosity) and large overall dimensions. The SH sample shows remarkably broad, tall, and AP-expanded pelvises. The total length of the sacrum and of the complete hip bone, and of the ischium, ilium, and pubis, the vertical acetabular diameter, and the breadth of the ilium and sacrum are conspicuously above MH ([_SI Appendix_, Table S18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). The SH pelvic remains are also distinct from MH in having an anteriorly located acetabulocristal buttress, a well-developed supraacetabular groove and a thin and rectangular, plate-like superior pubic ramus that contrasts with the thick and stout pubis of MH ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r10), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r25)) ([_SI Appendix_, Figs. S9 and S10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). These features, together with the very broad elliptical pelvis, are shared with early and middle Pleistocene _Homo_ specimens, and they likely represent the plesiomorphic condition for the genus _Homo._

Neandertals depart from the SH pattern mainly in having an extreme craniocaudal flattening of the pubic ramus ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r10), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r11), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r25), [40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r40)). Neandertal pelvises, although broader than MH (probably due to prominent iliac flaring), are narrower than SH, likely related to a significantly smaller sacral breadth and iliac height in Neandertals ([_SI Appendix_, Table S18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). Unlike MH, the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) of the Neandertals is medially twisted relative to the anterior margin of the iliac blade and is bordered by a deep iliopsoas groove that excavates the medial surface of the AIIS ([41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r41), [42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r42)). This AIIS configuration agrees with that found in the SH sample ([Fig. 2 _D_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig02)) and other middle Pleistocene hip bones ([43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r43)). In contrast, the iliopsoas groove in hip bones of earlier _Homo_ taxa is shallow and does not excavate the medial surface of the AIIS ([44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r44)).

The SH femora show the plesiomorphic morphological pattern found in most earlier members of the genus _Homo_ ([45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r45)–[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r47)). The SH femora have relatively longer and, on average, moderately AP-flattened necks, ML-widened proximal (subtrochanteric) shaft, relatively low-neck-shaft angle, large gluteal ridges, well-developed hypotrochanteric fossae and proximal lateral crest, absence of a true pilaster, very low point of minimum shaft breadth, and thicker cortical bone than in MH ([Figs. 1 _D_ and _E_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01) and [2 _E_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig02) and [_SI Appendix_, Fig. S11 and Tables S19–S22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).

The SH tibiae share a similar morphological pattern with Neandertals that includes large retroversion angle of the proximal epiphysis ([_SI Appendix_, Fig. S12 and Tables S19–S22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)), tibial condyles located in a more posterior position in relation to the axis of the shaft, and flat proximal and distal articular surfaces. Distally, there is moderate hypertrophy of the medial malleolus and presence of squatting facets in some adult specimens (25%), related by some researchers to a hyperdorsiflexion of the ankle joint ([48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r48)). The robusticity of the fibula overlaps the upper range for MH.

In all of the anatomical details of the upper and lower limb, the SH immature individuals follow the same pattern as in the adult specimens ([_SI Appendix_, Tables S14 and S20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).

### Foot.

Despite subtle variation in Pleistocene hominin tali, some consistent morphological variants can be identified among different fossil samples ([27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r27), [49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r49)). The Neandertal talus displays broader lateral malleolar facets ([50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r50)) and talar heads compared with MH. In the SH specimens, the peroneal facet is significantly broader ([Fig. 2 _F_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig02)) and the talar head narrower than both Neandertals and MH ([_SI Appendix_, Table S23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). In SH, as in Neandertals, the trochlea is relatively broad with parallel sides, compared with the relatively narrow and wedge-shaped trochlea of MH ([27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r27), [49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r49)) ([Fig. 1 _F_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01)). Finally, all Pleistocene (non-_H. sapiens_) fossil tali, including SH, show a tall trochlea compared with recent MH, allowing for a greater capacity for dorsiflexion and plantarflexion of the ankle joint ([51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r51)).

The calcanei of Neandertals are broad with a projected sustentaculum tali and a long calcaneal tuber ([39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r39)). In SH, the calcanei are also broad and the sustentaculum tali is even more projected ([28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r28)).

The metatarsals from SH, Neandertals, and MH are very similar except for the broader base of the lateral metatarsals (MTIII–V), a potentially derived character shared between SH and Neandertals ([49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r49)). The SH proximal pedal phalanges present hypertrophy of the shaft, and the distal phalanx of the big toe shows an expanded distal tuberosity, as in the Neandertals ([39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r39), [52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r52)).

[](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/)Discussion
---------------------------------------------------------------

### Implications for Evolution of Body Size and Shape.

The SH hominins could be included within the “wide _Homo_” bauplan due to their absolutely and relatively large and ML-wide biotype consisting of a large thorax with broad shoulders and pelvises, above-medium-height body, thick bones, and great musculature and body mass. This body shape is also largely present in other early and middle Pleistocene individuals and in Neandertals. We base this hypothesis on the Jinniushan pelvis ([12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r12)) as well as on the similarity of the SH coxal bone with KNM-ER 3228, OH28, Arago 44, and Kabwe E.719 ([53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r53)). Our analysis suggests that three aspects of this biotype (body breadth, stature, and weight) show a mosaic pattern of evolution ([Fig. 1 _A_–_C_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01) and [_SI Appendix_, Table S24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)) ([54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r54), [55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r55)).

Although there are no known pelvic remains attributed to _H. habilis_, in our view, a ML relatively wide biotype was likely present (as the most parsimonious interpretation) in the earliest members of the genus _Homo_ and was inherited from their early hominin ancestors. Variation in this width within the genus _Homo_ has been proposed to follow a latitudinal cline, similar to that present in modern humans ([56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r56)). This great width of the pelvis may also have had obstetric implications, including a nonrotational delivery ([56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r56), [57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r57)). However, in SH Pelvis 1 the AP diameters of the pelvic canal are similar or even larger than in modern males, and a rotational delivery has been proposed ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r10), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r25)).

About 1.6–1.5 Mya some individuals began to show an increase in stature, reaching heights comparable to those present in middle-latitude MH populations. Direct evidence, based on femoral head size, of heavier bodies appears later, during the middle Pleistocene (including the SH population) and is retained in Neandertals. Body mass estimations based on other parameters such as the BIB-stature or cortical thickness, as well as the size and shape of some African femoral and pelvic remains (KNM-ER 736, 737, 1808, 3228, KNM-WT 15000, OH 28, and 34) suggest that tall and heavy bodies were present even earlier. Thus, the bauplan in the genus _Homo_ seems to have been characterized by a long period of stasis during which the “wide” (with respect to their stature) body plan shared by different _Homo_ species (including the SH hominins) varied rather little throughout the Pleistocene until the appearance of the new “narrow” bauplan in _H. sapiens_ ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r10), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r25), [26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r26)). The appearance of this “narrow” bauplan has energetic implications, which have been invoked as one of the reasons for the success of our species ([58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r58)), although the major change in relative skeletal strength (lower-limb diaphyseal cross-sectional geometry) within _Homo_ may have taken place after, not at, the origin of _H. sapiens_ ([59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r59)).

### Pattern of Evolution of the Postcranial Anatomical Traits.

The preservation of all anatomical parts in SH has allowed a detailed characterization of the postcranial anatomy and has revealed that the SH hominins share many anatomical features with Neandertals not present in MH. These could be Neandertal specializations, but the scant fossil record of postcranial elements in early Pleistocene _Homo_ makes it difficult to establish a clear cladistic polarity for many anatomical features, such as the morphology of the axis, the proximal humerus, the ulna, or the tibia. Some traits whose polarity can be established seem to be mainly plesiomorphic retentions in the SH hominins because they are already present in earlier _Homo_ specimens, such as the general morphology of the pelvis and femur or the talar trochlea. Therefore, these traits do not phylogenetically relate the SH population with Neandertals.

A few features that have been considered Neandertal-derived traits are also present in the SH hominins, including a low degree of lumbar lordosis, broad distal tuberosities of the manual phalanges, and the wide bases of the lateral metatarsals (MTIII–V), which is consistent with the hypothesis, based on the cranial morphology, that the SH hominins are a sister group to the later Neandertals ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r16)).

In addition, there are some Neandertal specializations that are not present in the SH hominins, such as the lateral orientation of the lumbar transverse processes, the less saddle-shaped carpo-metacarpal articulation of the thumb, and the extremely thin, plate-like superior pubic ramus. Finally, some taxonomically relevant traits are polymorphic in SH, although the Neandertal condition is dominant. These features include, among others, the general radius morphology (neck length, radial tuberosity orientation, and diaphyseal curvature), the morphology of the axillary border of the scapula, and the shape of the distal humerus. The presence of these polymorphisms in the SH sample and their fixation in the Neandertals suggests that a subsequent loss of variation occurred in the latter.

The detailed postcranial anatomy in SH indicates that some of the potentially derived Neandertal features were not yet present in this population. Thus, the full suite of Neandertal features did not arise all at once, and the evolution of the postcranial skeleton could be characterized as following a mosaic pattern. A mosaic pattern was also documented in the SH cranium ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r16)) although, in this case, the Neandertal suite of derived features forms a single functional complex.

[](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/)Conclusions
----------------------------------------------------------------

In general, the body plan in the genus _Homo_ has been largely characterized by stasis since ∼1.6 Mya until the appearance of MH ([2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r2)). Individuals with tall, wide, and heavy bodies, compared with earlier hominins, were already present at this early date in Africa and (probably) Asia. A subsequent slight increase in body mass occurred only approximately 1 million years later in middle Pleistocene populations (including SH), and these body parameters were largely maintained in the Neandertals. Variation in body breadth in Pleistocene _Homo_ has been suggested to follow a latitudinal cline. Absolute and relative brain size increased between the early and the middle Pleistocene, as seen in the higher EQ in SH. This was followed by a subsequent further increase in the EQ in Neandertals and MH.

In sum, SH offers the best proxy for the general postcranial size and shape of _Homo_ for at least the past 1 million years until the appearance of MH. Despite large periods of morphological stasis in the general body plan, the anatomical details of the postcranial skeleton, as revealed in the SH sample, offer the best evidence for a pattern of mosaic evolution in the postcranium within the Neandertal lineage.

[](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/)Materials and Methods
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

The SH postcranial sample up to the 2013 field season is composed of 1,523 elements ([_SI Appendix_, Table S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). The comparative material used in this study is listed in [_SI Appendix_, Table S25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691). Additional information on materials can be found in [_SI Appendix_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691). To avoid methodological problems in estimating body size parameters in the genus _Homo_, we have generally used the raw values for femoral length, BIB, and FHD as proxies for stature, body breadth, and weight in our comparisons with other fossils ([Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01)). Additional information on the materials and methods for stature, body mass, intrapopulational size variation, and encephalization quotient can be found in [_SI Appendix_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).

5.title: The stratigraphy of the Sima de los Huesos (Atapuerca, Spain) and implications for the origin of the fossil hominin accumulation
5.content:
[![Image 1: Elsevier](https://www.sciencedirect.com/us-east-1/prod/216a598ba584ec7107ee673c5b628e3ab9d74d3b/image/elsevier-non-solus.svg)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/quaternary-international "Go to Quaternary International on ScienceDirect")

[![Image 2: Quaternary International](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1040618217X00141-cov150h.gif)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/quaternary-international/vol/433/part/PA)

Abstract
--------

The Sima de Los Huesos (SH) is one of the many archaeo-palaeontological sites in the Sierra de Atapuerca. The characteristics of this palaeoanthropological site are unusual, due to the large size of the hominin accumulation and its location far from the karst entrances, at least today. In order to investigate the [geological processes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/geological-process "Learn more about geological processes from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") involved in the site formation and their relation to the hominin deposit, we have performed a study of the stratigraphical sequence and depositional history of SH. Analysis and correlation of the identified layers has allowed us to redefine the depositional structure of the site based on twelve lithostratigraphic units, which can be further grouped into five allostratigraphic units delimited by erosional boundaries. The results show that there was only one stratigraphic event of hominin accumulation. Cave bears and other carnivores occur with the hominin [fossils](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/fossil "Learn more about fossils from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages") in the same layer, but carnivores continued accumulating above the hominin deposit in an overlying layer. Our findings also argue against the hypothesis that the hominin or carnivore bones were transported to SH from a locus of primary accumulation remote from their present day location. The present study also reveals that, at the time of the hominin and carnivore fossil accumulations, the only possible access to the SH chamber was a deep vertical conduit, which was impossible to climb.

Introduction
------------

Sima de los Huesos (SH) is a cave site that has yielded an astonishing number of Middle Pleistocene hominin fossils corresponding to a minimum of 28 individuals (Bermúdez de Castro et al., 2004). Given the skeletal part representation in the collection, composed of all anatomical parts (Arsuaga et al., 1997), it is likely that entire corpses were deposited at the site. How the skeletons accumulated there has been highly debated, and different hypotheses have been proposed: i) a catastrophic event (Díez, 1990, Aguirre, 2000); ii) the combined intervention of three agents: humans (collector agent), carnivores (transport agent) and mass transport as mud flow (reworking agent) (Andrews and Fernández-Jalvo, 1997) and iii) the intentional accumulation of corpses inside the chamber (Arsuaga et al., 1990, Arsuaga et al., 1997, Arsuaga and Martínez, 2004). Recent taphonomic studies rule out the carnivores as accumulation agents, since tooth marks are rare in the hominin collection (Sala et al., 2014), and the pattern of fractures on the long bones indicates that the vast majority occurred after burial and were caused by the overlying sediment pressure (Sala et al., 2015). According to Andrews and Fernández Jalvo (1997), the arrival of human remains to the SH chamber was, in part, due to a geological agent (mud flow). Since this hypothesis was developed mainly from a taphonomic perspective, the study of the site stratigraphy can shed light on this issue. Therefore, understanding the stratigraphy of the Sima de los Huesos site and of the infilling processes is necessary to gain insight into the origin of the hominin bone accumulation.

Previous papers have dealt with the geology and geochronology of the SH site (Arsuaga et al., 1993, Arsuaga et al., 1997, Arsuaga et al., 2014, Bischoff et al., 1997, Bischoff et al., 2003, Bischoff et al., 2007, Parés et al., 2000, Arnold et al., 2014). Studies conducted during recent field seasons at SH have largely corroborated previous descriptions of the stratigraphic units. These latest studies have focused on the spatio-temporal relationship of the different lithostratigraphic levels, the sedimentologic characterization and on the reconstruction of geological processes. Building on these efforts, the present study aims to: i) provide a comprehensive description of the SH infill stratigraphy; ii) reconstruct the geological formation processes; and iii) interpret the origin of the sediments and fossil-bearing deposits.

Section snippets
----------------

Geographical and geological setting
-----------------------------------

The Sierra de Atapuerca is located in the northeast area of the Cenozoic Duero Basin (north-central Iberian Peninsula), which is delimited to the north and southeast by the Alpine orogens of the Cantabrian and Iberian Ranges, and within the Bureba Corridor. The Sierra de Atapuerca is an anticline ridge (1078 m asl) over the valley of the Arlanzón river (Benito and Pérez-González, 2014).

The bedrock of the Sierra de Atapuerca consists of grey-dark micritic marine limestone and dolomite deposited

Material and methods
--------------------

Six stratigraphic columns and five lithostratigraphic sections have been drawn (using tape measure and total station to obtain the spatial coordinates) for SR and SH (Fig.3, Fig.4) along 18 m lengthwise and subsequently digitalized using Macromedia FreeHand 10 software. Stratigraphy and sediment characterization
------------------------------------------

Analysis and correlation of the identified layers has allowed us to redefine the depositional structure of the site based on twelve lithostratigraphic units (LU), which can be further grouped into five allostratigraphic units (AU) delimited by erosional boundaries (Fig.3, Fig.4). The new revised sedimentological scheme expands on previously published descriptions (Arsuaga et al., 1993, Arsuaga et al., 1997, Arsuaga et al., 2014, Bischoff et al., 1997). The sedimentological description of each

Hominin bone deposit
--------------------

The first issue to be addressed is whether the SH hominin fossils belong to a single geological event (regardless of how much time elapsed from the deposition of the first fossil until that of the last fossil) or if they accumulated in two or more geological episodes (i.e., lying in two or more layers).

We can confidently state that there is only one hominin fossil event in SH because a number of hominin cranial fragments and teeth from SRA, SRM and SRB, as well as from the excavation squares

Conclusions
-----------

The origin of the Sima de los Huesos hominin accumulation is one of the most debated issues in paleoanthropology. A complete understanding of the sedimentological features of the deposit is necessary to clarify the role of the geological processes in the fossil accumulation. 1.title: Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins
1.description: Nuclear DNA sequences from Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins show they were more closely related to Neanderthals than to Denisovans, and indicate a population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans that predates 430,000 years ago. This genomic analysis of Middle Pleistocene hominins from Sima de los Huesos in the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain shows that they were more closely related to Neanderthals than to Denisovans, and indicates a divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans that predates 430,000 years ago. A previous report based on analyses of mitochondrial genomes from these specimens had suggested close relationship to Denisovans, which was in contrast to other archaeological evidence including morphological features shared with Late Pleistocene Neanderthals. A unique assemblage of 28 hominin individuals, found in Sima de los Huesos in the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain, has recently been dated to approximately 430,000 years ago1. An interesting question is how these Middle Pleistocene hominins were related to those who lived in the Late Pleistocene epoch, in particular to Neanderthals in western Eurasia and to Denisovans, a sister group of Neanderthals so far known only from southern Siberia. While the Sima de los Huesos hominins share some derived morphological features with Neanderthals, the mitochondrial genome retrieved from one individual from Sima de los Huesos is more closely related to the mitochondrial DNA of Denisovans than to that of Neanderthals2. However, since the mitochondrial DNA does not reveal the full picture of relationships among populations, we have investigated DNA preservation in several individuals found at Sima de los Huesos. Here we recover nuclear DNA sequences from two specimens, which show that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were related to Neanderthals rather than to Denisovans, indicating that the population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans predates 430,000 years ago. A mitochondrial DNA recovered from one of the specimens shares the previously described relationship to Denisovan mitochondrial DNAs, suggesting, among other possibilities, that the mitochondrial DNA gene pool of Neanderthals turned over later in their history.

Abstract
--------

A unique assemblage of 28 hominin individuals, found in Sima de los Huesos in the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain, has recently been dated to approximately 430,000 years ago[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17405#ref-CR1 "Arsuaga, J. L. et al. Neandertal roots: cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos. Science 344, 1358–1363 (2014)"). An interesting question is how these Middle Pleistocene hominins were related to those who lived in the Late Pleistocene epoch, in particular to Neanderthals in western Eurasia and to Denisovans, a sister group of Neanderthals so far known only from southern Siberia. While the Sima de los Huesos hominins share some derived morphological features with Neanderthals, the mitochondrial genome retrieved from one individual from Sima de los Huesos is more closely related to the mitochondrial DNA of Denisovans than to that of Neanderthals[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17405#ref-CR2 "Meyer, M. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014)"). However, since the mitochondrial DNA does not reveal the full picture of relationships among populations, we have investigated DNA preservation in several individuals found at Sima de los Huesos. Here we recover nuclear DNA sequences from two specimens, which show that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were related to Neanderthals rather than to Denisovans, indicating that the population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans predates 430,000 years ago. A mitochondrial DNA recovered from one of the specimens shares the previously described relationship to Denisovan mitochondrial DNAs, suggesting, among other possibilities, that the mitochondrial DNA gene pool of Neanderthals turned over later in their history.

Editorial Summary
-----------------

### Neanderthal-like hominins in Middle Pleistocene Spain

This genomic analysis of Middle Pleistocene hominins from Sima de los Huesos in the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain shows that they were more closely related to Neanderthals than to Denisovans, and indicates a divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans that predates 430,000 years ago. A previous report based on analyses of mitochondrial genomes from these specimens had suggested close relationship to Denisovans, which was in contrast to other archaeological evidence including morphological features shared with Late Pleistocene Neanderthals.

6.title: New bracketing luminescence ages constrain the Sima de los Huesos hominin fossils (Atapuerca, Spain) to MIS 12
6.content:
Introduction
------------

Located within the deep chambers of the Sierra de Atapuerca karst system (northern Spain), the Sima de los Huesos (SH) site has yielded thousands of hominin fossils (Arsuaga et al., 1997a) and represents the largest individual Middle Pleistocene fossil assemblage for the genus _Homo_ globally. In total, more than 6900 fossils relating to at least 28 individuals have been excavated from a single stratigraphic level (Bermúdez de Castro et al., 2004, Aranburu et al., 2017). Nuclear DNA sequencing and cranial morphological analyses of these fossils have firmly placed the SH hominins at the beginning of the Neandertal lineage (Arsuaga et al., 2014, Meyer et al., 2016) and have shown a mosaic pattern of evolution, with certain Neandertal specializations (teeth, face, temporomandibular joint and occipital bone) arising earlier than other Neandertal apomorphies. The SH fossils are also associated with an Acheulean handaxe, making SH one of the few archaeological sites worldwide for which this iconic lithic industry can be directly related to a specific hominin group (Carbonell and Mosquera, 2006, Daura et al., 2017). Establishing firm minimum and maximum ages for the SH fossils using numerical dating techniques is therefore important for understanding the evolutionary and cultural history of these individuals, and their temporal relationships with other Early and Middle Pleistocene hominin records from Europe.

The completeness of the skeletal representation in the SH hominin assemblage, which preserves all anatomical components (Arsuaga et al., 1997a), is consistent with the interpretation that entire corpses were deposited at the site, either as accidental falls or as intentional anthropic accumulations. However, the origins and accumulation mechanisms of the SH hominins remain widely debated, with proposed hypotheses ranging from catastrophic events (Díez, 1990, Aguirre, 2000), the combined intervention of humans (collector agent), carnivores (transport agent) and mud flows (reworking agent; Andrews and Fernández-Jalvo, 1997), other undetermined natural causes (Egeland et al., 2018), and the intentional accumulation of corpses inside the chamber (Arsuaga et al., 1993, Arsuaga et al., 1997a, Arsuaga and Martínez, 2004). Several recent geological, taphonomic and forensic studies have refuted a number of these proposed hypotheses. In particular, it has been shown that the sedimentological features of the hominin-bearing unit (well-sorted, homogeneous muds devoid of extraclasts) do not support the hypothesis that the hominin bones were geologically transported to SH from a distant locus of primary accumulation (Aranburu et al., 2017). Recent taphonomic studies have also suggested that carnivores were not the primary accumulation agents (Sala et al., 2014). Additionally, analysis of long bone fracture patterns has indicated that the vast majority of such breakages occurred after burial and were caused by overlying sediment pressure, while analysis of cranial fractures does not support an accidental cause of hominin accumulation in the SH chamber (Sala et al., 2015a, Sala et al., 2015b, Sala et al., 2016). Although it is difficult to determine the exact causes, duration (over human timescales) and nature (synchronous versus repeated events) of hominin fossil accumulation at SH, it has been possible to demonstrate that the hominin fossil deposit represents a single accumulation episode on lithostratigraphic grounds (Aranburu et al., 2017). In this sense, the >28 individuals represented in the SH record have been considered to belong to the same biological population, a paleodeme. The existence of such a well-preserved and complete paleodeme at SH has provided unique opportunities for studying Neandertal evolution based on a large collection of individuals from the same group, instead of relying on a series of isolated specimens from disparate localities.

Detailed anatomical studies of the SH collection led Arsuaga et al. (2014) to conclude that there was a mosaic pattern of cranial evolution in Neandertals, with different anatomical and functional modules evolving at different rates. This interpretation was based on the fact that the derived Neandertal traits are not uniformly distributed in the cranial anatomy of the SH collection. Instead, Neandertal traits concentrate in a few regions of the cranium and are consistently observed throughout the entire SH paleodeme, while other cranial regions lack Neandertal specializations and are considered primitive. The most clear Neandertal apomorphies in the SH collection are found in the facial skeleton, including the mandible and teeth, as well as the temporomandibular joint (Arsuaga et al., 2014). The simultaneous occurrence of these apomorphies suggests that they are functionally related and are part of the same adaptation, which probably reflects a masticatory specialization in early Neandertals. A similar mosaic pattern has been attributed to the evolution of modern humans based on the Jebel Irhoud fossils, which have been radiometrically dated to 315±34 ka (Hublin et al., 2017, Richter et al., 2017). Here again, modern human face, mandible and teeth specializations have evolved earlier than neurocranium apomorphies, albeit in a different direction to that of Neandertals. Thus, Neandertals and modern humans appear to have followed a similar evolutionary mosaic pattern, one that could be described as ‘face first, brain later’. Although the Jebel Irhoud fossils are younger than those at SH (Arsuaga et al., 2014, Richter et al., 2017), determining a precise bracketing age for the SH hominins is important not only to establish when the Neandertal clade branched out, but also to determine when the different morphofunctional units (modules) arose, and to appropriately compare the patterns and timing of evolution in Neandertals and modern humans.

Improved chronological constraints on the SH assemblage are also critical for determining how past environmental change may have influenced hominin biological and cultural evolution over glacial-interglacial cycles, particularly those pertaining to the Middle Pleistocene Neandertal lineage (e.g., Dennell et al., 2011, Hérisson et al., 2016, Bermúdez de Castro et al., 2016, Roebroeks and Soressi, 2016). Orbitally-driven climate change has often been invoked as a major factor controlling Neandertal evolution in Europe via population expansions and crashes associated with glacial retractions and advances (Hublin and Roebroeks, 2009). According to Hublin (2009:16025), “The fossil record suggests that the cold episode(s) that triggered the process of divergence of the Neandertal clade most likely predates OIS 11”. During past glacial stages, icecap and permafrost advances in northern Europe are thought to have rendered large parts of the continent potentially uninhabitable and would have restricted hominin populations to the Mediterranean peninsulas (Dennell et al., 2011). This arrangement would have likely led to the fragmentation of human groups across a quasi-discontinuous habitable territory. The subsequent retreat of glaciers during interglacial stages would have led to population expansion and an increased chance for admixture among different human groups (e.g., Dennell et al., 2011; Steward and Stringer, 2012). It is predicted that these repeated cycles of population expansion and contraction during the Middle Pleistocene lead to enhanced hominin diversity in Europe and a non-anagenetic pattern of evolution (i.e., a pattern that was not gradual and did not involve a single human population), since anagenetic evolution requires climatic stability over a continuous geographic region. Indeed, the emerging picture from the European Middle Pleistocene hominin fossil record suggests that a non-anagenetic (likely cladogenetic) model is better suited to describe the pattern of hominin evolution on the continent. In particular, hominin fossils that are potentially contemporaneous with, or even younger than, those from SH, such as the Ceprano (∼353 ka; Nomade et al., 2011, Manzi et al., 2011) or Arago (∼450 ka, Falguères et al., 2015) specimens, show less derived Neandertal conditions, while the Aroeira cranium from Portugal, which has been dated to 436–390 ka, shows a combination of Neandertal traits that is different to that observed at SH (Daura et al., 2017; Conde-Valverde et al., 2018). Clearly, a more refined timeline and further accurate dating of Middle Pleistocene hominin fossils are necessary to reliably unravel these complex phylogeographic patterns.

Obtaining reliable and precise chronologies for Middle Pleistocene archaeological sites has traditionally proved difficult due to the limited number of radiometric dating techniques that are applicable over this time-period (>125 ka) and because suitable dating materials are not always readily available in stratigraphic association with target horizons. In this sense, the ubiquitous presence of silicate minerals at most archaeological sites makes luminescence dating a viable option for indirectly dating biological remains and cultural artifacts. Advances in luminescence dating over the last decade have also opened up new possibilities for obtaining finite and reliable age estimates on Middle Pleistocene sedimentary deposits (e.g., Duller and Wintle, 2012, Li et al., 2014, Arnold et al., 2015, Arnold et al., 2016), with at least two novel signals offering good potential for circumventing the limited upper age limit of conventional optically stimulated luminescence (OSL); namely, thermally-transferred OSL (TT-OSL) signals from quartz grains (Wang et al., 2006a, Wang et al., 2006b) and post infrared (IR) stimulated luminescence (i.e., pIR-IRSL) signals from K-rich feldspar grains (Thomsen et al., 2008, Buylaert et al., 2012). Numerous paleoanthropological and archaeological sites in Europe have now been dated using these methods (e.g., Rink et al., 2013, Frouin et al., 2014, Hernandez et al., 2014, Demuro et al., 2015, Ollé et al., 2016, Arriolabengoa et al., 2018). Furthermore, the reliability of these techniques have been successfully tested on several independently or semi-independently dated stratigraphic sections from the Sierra de Atapuerca archaeological complex (Arnold et al., 2013, Arnold et al., 2015, Demuro et al., 2014, Demuro et al., 2019), and confirm that the luminescence properties of host deposits from this geological province are generally well-suited for single-grain TT-OSL and multi-grain pIR-IRSL dating (e.g., Arnold et al., 2019). Systematic investigations of single-grain TT-OSL properties have revealed that some sediment layers at Atapuerca can contain subpopulations of quartz grains with unsuitable TT-OSL responses, including low thermal stabilities that can give rise to age underestimation if equivalent dose (D e) measurements are made on multi-grain aliquots (Arnold and Demuro, 2015). To circumvent this problem, and to avoid other types of averaging effects that may arise from simultaneously measuring grains with different bleaching histories, signal compositions or TT-OSL source trap properties, Arnold and Demuro (2015) recommended performing TT-OSL D e measurements at the individual grain scale where possible. The present study adopts these recommendations, and focuses on single-grain TT-OSL dating to establish new age constraint on the SH fossil deposits.

To reliably constrain the age of the SH hominins by luminescence dating requires firm knowledge of the stratigraphic relationships of target sediments associated with, and surrounding, the human fossils, as well as confidence in the overall stratigraphic integrity of the site (Rodríguez-Rey et al., 2015). Detailed prior sedimentological analysis undertaken at SH suggests that deposition of the fossils and the encasing sediment (the red clays) occurred coevally, and that any postdepositional movements within the chamber have been restricted to minor and localized events (Aranburu et al., 2017). The latter interpretations are further supported by the relatively homogenous single-grain TT-OSL D e distributions obtained for overlying SH deposits (Arnold et al., 2014). Similarly, there are no signs of re-transportation or postdepositional alteration of the human fossils found at the base of the SH chamber (Aranburu et al., 2017). These stratigraphical and taphonomic considerations indicate that luminescence dating of the red clay (LU-5 and LU-6) deposition event should provide unambiguous and tightly associated age constraint on the SH hominin fossils.

Previous luminescence dating attempts at SH have focused exclusively on a debris flow deposit known as Café con Leche (LU-7), which is found throughout the SH chamber and directly overlies the hominin fossil-bearing red clays (Arnold et al., 2014, Arsuaga et al., 2014). This study aims to build on the existing minimum age estimates for the SH assemblage and to better constrain the timing for the onset of Neandertal speciation by establishing a more precise bracketing chronology (i.e., a maximum age, as well as a coeval age) for the hominin remains. To this end, we report on new luminescence dating (single-grain TT-OSL) results obtained for the sediment layers that encase and directly underlie the hominin accumulations (LU-6 and LU-5). We also derive combined age estimates for each depositional phase at SH by constructing a Bayesian model using our latest dating results and previously published chronologies. In addressing important existing gaps in the SH chronological record, we go on to discuss the climatic context of early Neandertal evolution in Europe and examine the complex evolutionary histories and phylogenetic relationships between SH and other European Middle Pleistocene hominin records.

The population at the Sima de los Huesos rises to 29 individuals
----------------------------------------------------------------

Thursday, 05 November 2020

_The CENIEH publishes a paper on the 7600 human fossils found at this site in the Sierra de Atapuerca, confirming that this Middle Pleistocene population was made up of 29 individuals instead of the 28 considered in earlier studies._

[](https://facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals)

[](https://twitter.com/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals&text=The%20population%20at%20the%20Sima%20de%20los%20Huesos%20rises%20to%2029%20individuals%20%7C%20CENIEH)

[](https://plus.google.com/share?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals)

[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals)

[](whatsapp://send?text=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals%20The%20population%20at%20the%20Sima%20de%20los%20Huesos%20rises%20to%2029%20individuals%20%7C%20CENIEH)

[](http://www.meneame.net/submit.php?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals)

[](mailto:?subject=The%20population%20at%20the%20Sima%20de%20los%20Huesos%20rises%20to%2029%20individuals%20%7C%20CENIEH&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cenieh.es%2Fen%2Fpress%2Fnews%2Fpopulation-sima-de-los-huesos-rises-29-individuals)

[](javascript:window.print())

![Image 6: Mandible AT-2 from Sima de los Huesos/M. Modesto](https://www.cenieh.es/sites/default/files/styles/max_325x325/public/noticia/images/Figure%203.png?itok=spcolQY5)

José Mª Bermúdez de Castro, coordinator of the Paleobiology Program at the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH), has led a paper just published in the journal _[Anatomical Record](https://anatomypubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ar.24551)_ on the population at the Sima de los Huesos site, in the Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos, Spain), which confirms that this Middle Pleistocene human group was comprised of 29 individuals, instead of the 28 estimated in earlier studies.

During the 2019 excavation campaign, the impressive total of 7600 human fossils from the Sima de los Huesos was reached, forming a collection unique in the world for studying the variability of a past species. In 2003, when the number of fossils stood at 4000, it had been calculated that 28 different individuals were represented.

During recent excavation campaigns, very complete bone remains have been encountered, as well as others that have allowed craniums, jaws and postcranial skeleton bones to be reconstructed. For this reason, it appeared necessary to carry out another demographic study of the Sima de los Huesos, and this took place in January 2020, starting with the hypothesis that the number of individuals in the collection could have increased significantly. Nevertheless, and surprisingly, the estimated number of individuals has only risen from 28 to 29.

“We have been able to verify that some individuals have been becoming more complete, while others are still represented by the same teeth and jaw fragments recovered during the first years of excavation”, says Bermúdez de Castro. “It appears to be clear that the damage to the site before the 1976 discovery of the first human fossils was major and a lot of information about some individuals has been lost”, adds the co-director of Atapuerca.

![Image 7: dos dientes de la Sima de los Huesos, AT-11 y AT-12/M. Modesto](https://www.cenieh.es/sites/default/files/inline-images/Figure%201.png)
**Sex and age**

In addition, the sex of the individuals from the Sima de los Huesos was reviewed in this work. It is estimated that nine of them could be male and fifteen female. Despite this imbalance, the statistical analyses concluded that the 8:15 ratio could have come from a population in which both sexes were equally represented.

Moreover, there is an excess of teenagers and very young adults (82.8%). Only one child individual has been recorded, while four adults had reached maturity, possibly in the age range 40 to 45.

“With such high mortality at such young ages, the reproductive viability of a Pleistocene hunter-gatherer group could not be sustained. Given that the overall mortality at the Sima de los Huesos matches a catastrophic profile better, it is possible that their lives were ended by a single event of unknown type”, says Bermúdez de Castro.

Abstract
--------

After 34 years of research and findings in the Middle Pleistocene site of the Sima de los Huesos (SH) of the Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos, Spain), we present an update of the estimation of the number of individuals (ENI) identified in the SH hominin assemblage. The last ENI, published in 2004, was 28. Although the number of specimens recovered has almost doubled since then and more complete information is now available, this new analysis suggests that the ENI is 29. Some individuals are still represented by only one or a few teeth and the upper and lower jaws of various individuals have not been completed. We suggest that the amateur cavers, who accessed the SH site for years looking for bear fossils, destroyed a significant number of hominin fossils. Despite this, we have a good picture of the group of hominins represented in the SH assemblage. Because complete corpses were accumulated in SH and it is a closed cavity, it is expected that a significant number of hominin fossils remains to be discovered. According to the previous estimates, the representation of females is greater than that of males. However, the observed sex ratio is not significantly different from the 1:1 ratio. With the exception of the possible presence of a child individual, most of the remaining 28 individuals are teenagers or young adults (24/28 = 0.857). The ages of death of SH hominins appear to conform to a catastrophic profile.

**Keywords:** Sierra de Atapuerca; Sima de los Huesos; age at death; hominins; number of individuals; sex.

7.title: Lethal Interpersonal Violence in the Middle Pleistocene
7.description: Evidence of interpersonal violence has been documented previously in Pleistocene members of the genus Homo, but only very rarely has this been posited as the possible manner of death. Here we report the earliest evidence of lethal interpersonal violence in the hominin fossil record. Cranium 17 recovered from the Sima de los Huesos Middle Pleistocene site shows two clear perimortem depression fractures on the frontal bone, interpreted as being produced by two episodes of localized blunt force trauma. The type of injuries, their location, the strong similarity of the fractures in shape and size, and the different orientations and implied trajectories of the two fractures suggest they were produced with the same object in face-to-face interpersonal conflict. Given that either of the two traumatic events was likely lethal, the presence of multiple blows implies an intention to kill. This finding shows that the lethal interpersonal violence is an ancient human behavior and has important implications for the accumulation of bodies at the site, supporting an anthropic origin.

Abstract
--------

Evidence of interpersonal violence has been documented previously in Pleistocene members of the genus _Homo_, but only very rarely has this been posited as the possible manner of death. Here we report the earliest evidence of lethal interpersonal violence in the hominin fossil record. Cranium 17 recovered from the Sima de los Huesos Middle Pleistocene site shows two clear perimortem depression fractures on the frontal bone, interpreted as being produced by two episodes of localized blunt force trauma. The type of injuries, their location, the strong similarity of the fractures in shape and size, and the different orientations and implied trajectories of the two fractures suggest they were produced with the same object in face-to-face interpersonal conflict. Given that either of the two traumatic events was likely lethal, the presence of multiple blows implies an intention to kill. This finding shows that the lethal interpersonal violence is an ancient human behavior and has important implications for the accumulation of bodies at the site, supporting an anthropic origin.

Introduction
------------

Interpersonal violence (lethal and nonlethal) in prehistory is of special interest since it provides a window into human social relations in the past and may be associated with subsistence contexts such as competition for scarce resources, population density or territorial defense [[1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref001)–[2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref002)]. Interpersonal violence can be manifested in different ways in the archaeological record, including trauma on hominin bones, which makes it susceptible to approach these questions in paleoanthropological contexts through the application of modern forensic methods of trauma analysis. Interpersonal violence is well-documented since at least Neolithic times [[3](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref003)–[5](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref005)]. In recent prehistory, perimortem human manipulation in the form of cutmarks or bone breakage patterns has often been interpreted as cannibalism [[6](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref006)–[9](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref009)] and could indicate violence between human social groups [[10](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref010)]. Evidence of cannibalism and defleshing is also present during the Paleolithic and has been documented in fossil hominins dating to at least the Early Pleistocene [[11](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref011)–[14](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref014)]. Nevertheless, there is no evidence of direct traumatic injury as a possible cause of death in any of these Pleistocene cases.

Cranial and postcranial trauma are relatively common among Middle and Upper Pleistocene hominins and in most cases show signs of healing ([S1 Table](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.s001)), indicating survival of the individual [[15](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref015)–[18](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref018)]. Currently, there are only two examples in the fossil record that are tentatively considered cases of lethal interpersonal violence. The Shanidar 3 Neandertal shows a penetrating lesion to the left ninth rib consisting of a parallel-sided groove with exostoses along its margins [[19](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref019)]. Nevertheless, some bone remodelling is apparent, suggesting this individual survived for several weeks after the lesion, and it is not clear that the final cause of death was related to the rib injury. The Upper Paleolithic _Homo sapiens_ individual Sunghir 1 shows a perimortem sharp trauma in the first thoracic vertebra that has been interpreted as the likely cause of death. While this would seem to represent a relatively clear case of lethal interpersonal violence, the authors did not rule out the possibility of a hunting accident [[20](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref020)]. Here we report on the presence of perimortem lethal cranial traumatic lesions in a Middle Pleistocene individual from the Sima de los Huesos (SH) site, a singular case in the hominin fossil record.

The SH site has yielded an extraordinarily large sample of Middle Pleistocene (c. 430 kya) hominin fossils belonging to the Neandertal clade [[21](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref021)] and corresponding to a minimum of 28 individuals [[22](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref022)]. During the time the hominin bones accumulated at the SH site, the only possible access route to the site were through a deep (13 m) vertical chimney [[23](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref023)]. Given the skeletal part representation in the collection [[24](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref024)], it is likely that entire bodies were deposited at the site. There are no cutmarks on any of the 6700+ hominin bones recovered to date, and carnivore manipulation (tooth marks) of the bones is rare [[25](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref025)]. The origin of the accumulation has been highly debated, and four different hypotheses (carnivore activity, transport by geological agents, accidental falls, and intentional accumulation of bodies by hominins) have been proposed [[24](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref024),[26](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref026)–[29](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref029)].

Recent taphonomic studies have ruled out carnivores and geological processes as accumulation agents [[23](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref023),[25](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref025),[30](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref030)]. The sediment of the hominin deposit (Lithostratigraphic Unit-6, LU-6) is indicative of a low-energy depositional environment (decantation) ([Fig 1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g001)), and the small size of the SH site suggests only short-distance transport of the fossils within the site [[21](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref021),[23](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref023)]. Furthermore, the red clay of LU-6 is devoid of extraclasts which provides strong evidence that the fossils were not subjected to long-distance transport, but likely accumulated _in situ_ at the SH conduit [[23](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref023)]. The pattern of postcranial fractures in the assemblage indicates that the vast majority occurred after burial, and were caused by the overlying sediment pressure [[30](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref030)]. Nevertheless, a low proportion (around 4%) of postcranial perimortem fractures were found [[30](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref030)] and several cases of antemortem healed cranial injuries are also present in the SH sample [[31](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref031)] ([S1 Table](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.s001)).

Materials and Methods
---------------------

Cranium 17 (Cr-17) is a very complete specimen composed of 52 bone fragments preserving the complete facial skeleton, including the partial upper dentition (the right C 1 to M 3 and the left C 1 to M 2), the frontal bone, the sphenoid bone (missing only the body), the left parietal bone, the left temporal bone (lacking only the mastoid process) and most of the occipital bone. The preserved right M 3 is fully functional and shows only slight wear, indicating that Cr-17 belonged to a young adult individual [[21](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref021)]. Junta de Castilla y León (Burgos, Spain) is the repository of the fossil (Cr-17). All necessary permits (excavation permit granted by the Junta de Castilla y León) were obtained for the described study, which complied with all relevant regulations.

Observations of the fractures were made with a Nikon SMZ800 Stereoscopic light microscope, as well as a DINO-LITE digital microscope. Detailed images of the fractures were made with a Nikon Digital Sight DS-Fi1 camera.

### Contour and trajectory analysis of the traumas

3D imaging provides an opportunity to present critical aspects of cranial blunt force trauma [[32](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref032)], such as shape analysis [[33](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref033)], and to investigate plausible injury trajectories. Cr-17 was CT scanned in the coronal plane using an industrial XYLON MU 2000-CT scanner at the Universidad de Burgos (Spain) with scanner energy of 180 kV and 4 mA. Slice thickness was collimated to 0.5 mm, inter-slice spacing was 0.2 mm, and the approximate field of view was 225 mm. A total of 1108 slices was obtained as a 1024 x 1024 matrix of 32 bit Float format, with a final pixel size of 0.219 x 0.219 mm. A virtual (3D CT) model of the cranium was generated from the resulting slices using the Mimics 16.0 (Materialise N.V.) software package.

Both, fracture angle and cortical delamination were measured on the virtual reconstructions using Mimics 16.0 software tools. Fracture angle is the angle formed by the fracture surface and the bone cortical table, while cortical delamination or bevelling is the cleavage between the diploë and the inner/outer table.

The form of both of the fractures was analyzed in order to compare their contours. Relying on the virtual reconstruction of the cranium, ten equidistant points were placed along the preserved outlines of both traumatic fractures (T1 and T2). The first point was placed on the notch in each fracture, and the 3-D coordinates of all the points were recorded. The coordinates were then transferred to the Morphologika 2.5 software program to perform the superposition of the two outlines relying on the first landmark (the notch) as a reference point. The two fractures outlines were rotated and superimposed but were not rescaled, to permit comparison of the true size of the lesions.

In forensic cases, the impact trajectories are estimated following the vectors of the entrance/exit wounds [[34](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref034)], especially for gunshot wounds. In the present case, the trajectory of the impact for each fracture was established by creating a normal vector to the plane of the fracture defined by the points outlining its contour.

Results
-------

### SH Cranium-17 injuries

The 52 fragments that comprise Cr-17 show clear postmortem fractures along their edges ([Table 1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-t001), Figs [2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g002) and [3](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g003)) typical of a dry bone breakage pattern commonly found in fossils under diagenetic conditions. No evidence of carnivore manipulation, such as tooth marks, is present on this specimen [[25](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref025)]. On the left side of the frontal squama, this individual shows two sub-rectangular-shaped fractures, Trauma 1 (T1) and Trauma 2 (T2) ([Fig 2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g002)).

The bone fragments that comprise the Cr-17 vault, as well as in the entire SH neurocranial sample, show a clear dominance of straight/curved fracture outlines, right angles between the cortical table and surface of the fracture, jagged surfaces and absence of cortical delamination along the fracture edges ([Table 1](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-t001)). These are typical features of a dry bone breakage pattern, with fractures commonly considered as occurring postmortem in forensic cases (see [Table 2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-t002)) These criteria are applicable to the SH cranial collection, as well as the postcranial bones [[30](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone.0126589.ref030)]. The T1 and T2 fractures do not follow this dry bone breakage pattern.

Trauma 1 (T1) is located 16 mm lateral of bregma and 72 mm anterior to the coronal suture. Trauma 2 (T2) is located 30 mm lateral of bregma and 56 mm anterior to the coronal suture. Both T1 and T2 are connected and affect the inner and outer bone tables. On the ectocranial surface ([Fig 2B](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g002)), the outline of T1 is sharp, with well-defined borders, and shows fracture lines radiating from the center of the trauma involving both the external and internal tables. The fracture angle of T1 is oblique (32.5°-44.8°, [Fig 4](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g004)). A small, but distinct, notch is present along the superior border of the outline of T1 on the ectocranial surface ([Fig 2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g002)). On the endocranial surface there is a halo of cortical delamination ([Fig 2](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589#pone-0126589-g002)) that varies from a minimum of about 4.9 mm to a maximum of about 8.8 mm.
